articles.title: Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?
articles.summary: Iran says the US bombed a wedding near the Strait of Hormuz; hits Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan in retaliation.
articles.body:
The United States and Iran have exchanged a new round of attacks – the biggest in more than a month – raising fears of escalation into a wider regional war.

The US Central Command said it struck dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Iran will be “totally wiped out” if it retaliates against the US attacks. “If they do respond, they’ll be hit much harder,” he told Fox News in an interview.

Iran has responded by firing ballistic missiles towards Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region. Tehran has accused the US of hitting a wedding party, killing at least four people.

Here is what’s happening in the US-Iran war.

Iran said that the US bombing of a house during a wedding celebration in the city of Kuhestak has killed at least four people. Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called it a “brutal” attack, where more than 68 people, including women and children, were wounded.

Footage published by the Iranian Red Crescent Society showed a building with walls and windows blown out, and debris scattered on the ground.

The humanitarian group also published pictures of several children receiving treatment at a hospital in Sirik, which overlooks the Strait of Hormuz.

In addition to Kuhestak, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported explosions in coastal cities including Konarak, Bandar Abbas, Jask, and Asaluyeh, as well as Qeshm Island.

The second consecutive night of US attacks comes as Washington is jostling to wrest control over the Strait of Hormuz, the global energy chokepoint, which remains under Iranian blockade and has become Tehran’s bargaining chip.

Two locations near the cities of Ahvaz and Aghajari in Iran’s southwestern Khuzestan province were hit in missile attacks, the province’s deputy governor for security affairs said, according to the state broadcaster IRIB.

Seven people were killed at three locations in the province, and eight others were injured in the attacks, the IRIB reported.

In total, at least 18 people have been killed across Iran.

Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq’s Erbil.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its forces carried out a combined missile and drone attack on US facilities in Erbil province in northern Iraq in retaliation for the US strike.

Iran claimed it hit the Sheikh Isa Airbase, which hosts US forces, in Bahrain. The IRGC said it launched a “heavy” ballistic missile attack on Prince Hassan airbase and a US Marine base in Jordan, and hit the headquarters and residence of the American commander of the Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait.

Tehran said its attack on Kuwait set fire to a drone hangar and a ramp through which UAVs participated in attacks on Iran, adding that several US drones were also destroyed, and claimed to have killed a number of US soldiers.

Kuwait reported intercepting drones and missiles but did not report any casualties. There was no immediate comment from Washington, either.

Jordanian armed forces said air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace earlier, with the remaining three falling in remote areas without causing casualties.

Washington and Tehran have upped the ante in attacks and political rhetoric amid a diplomatic deadlock. Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran will reciprocate if the US returns to the terms of the June Memorandum of Understanding that halted the military hostilities. The two sides have failed to agree before the deal expired on August 17.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said his country “has unforgettable lessons for the American enemy”.

Baghaei, the Iranian spokesman, called for global action against the US strike on the wedding function.

“This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it,” he said, pointing to attacks on the city of Minab and Lamerd on the first day of the war.

In Minab, US forces struck an elementary school, killing more than 150 people, and in Lamerd, they hit a sport hall, killing at least 21 people.

“Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness,” Baghaei said. “Still, those governments and international institutions that remain silent in the face of such barbarism, or seek to justify such acts, must understand that their silence is not neutrality.”

In the US, Trump said he is not trying to force Iran back to the negotiating table, dismissing reports that Washington is seeking a new agreement with Tehran.

“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

He added that Iran was “playing out the inevitable” and asked: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”

Alexandru Hudisteanu, a maritime security expert, told Al Jazeera that the recent escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran is unlikely to be a one-off “because this war has not been settled in military terms and both sides have the impetus to go to war from time to time”.

It can become “a repeatable pattern” although the war is no longer “in an active phase”, he said.

He added, “there are still conditions that create these flare-ups, especially because the US is trying to show that Iran does not have monolithic control over the Strait of Hormuz and on who passes through the strait.”

The talks over the status of Hormuz have been deadlocked, with Washington demanding an end to the Iranian blockade without any conditions while Tehran wants the US to end its naval blockade on its ports.

The latest escalation comes a week after the US imposed a slew of economic sanctions to pressure Iran to come to the negotiating table. Tehran says the US economic pressure will fail.

articles.title: Trump and Rubio’s bold Venezuela oil pact could finally crush communism’s grip
articles.summary: Critics call it colonialism, but the U.S.-Venezuela oil partnership aims to block Cuba, China and Russia from recapturing the failed state.
articles.body: For more than a quarter-century, Venezuela was not merely poorly governed. It was captured by Cuban communist intelligence services. Russian arms entrenched it. Chinese loans stripped the country of sovereignty while the Chávez–Maduro regime looted Venezuela, wrecked the currency and filled the prisons. The result was a failed state: mass exile, political prisoners, electrical blackouts and a platform for America’s enemies in the Western Hemisphere. That history is what critics of the new U.S.–Venezuela energy agreement prefer to forget. Last week, President Trump announced a historic oil partnership with Venezuela’s interim government. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth negotiated it. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez confirmed the core terms: 17 strategic fields holding more than 65 billion barrels, a production target above 1.5 million barrels a day, more than $100 billion in private investment and large fiscal flows to Venezuela. Whether the final term is a generation or a century-scale U.S. stake, the meaning is the same. The United States has taken a secured interest in the resource that once financed communism in Cuba and subversion all over Latin America. Previously, Venezuela’s oil was "sovereign" on paper and enslaved in practice — used to pay Cuban handlers, Russian weapons and Chinese debt while Venezuelans fled. Sovereignty without property rights, honest courts and a state that cannot be flipped by the Cuban communist regime is an empty word. TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES Critics on the left call the deal colonialism. Hard-line Chavistas call it betrayal. Parts of the opposition call it illegitimate because an interim government signed it. Democratic Socialists who treated Maduro as a diplomatic inconvenience suddenly discovered constitutional piety about hydrocarbons. They share a fantasy: that a weak, cash-starved, institutionally gutted Venezuela can stay free if Washington keeps its distance. History says otherwise: A vacuum in Venezuela is not filled by angels. It is filled by Cuban, Russian and Chinese intelligence, along with the criminal networks, like the Tren de Aragua, that grew up under the Venezuelan socialist regime and extended through the Western Hemisphere. That axis produced the torture chambers, the refugee crisis and the political prisons. A long-term U.S. commercial stake — backed by American security interests — is insurance. It raises the cost of a second communist capture. It makes it harder for a future corrupt regime to re-nationalize the industry overnight and resume shipping the crude to Cuba in exchange for rebuilding the repressive apparatus. American companies built much of that industry in the 20th century before Chávez confiscated it. The decay that followed was communist plunder. Reopening the oil fields under American capital and strategic oversight is how you prevent the next plunder. RUBIO WARNS CUBA HAS INFILTRATED US WITH SPIES, CALLS COMMUNIST REGIME AN 'ESPIONAGE SUPERPOWER' The deal must not become a substitute for liberty. Oil that merely finances the same repressive regime is not reconstruction. It is a richer dictatorship. Secretary Rubio has been clear since January, after the capture of Nicolás Maduro, that the United States would not occupy Venezuela. It would use leverage. The plan has three overlapping phases: stabilization, so the country does not collapse into war; recovery, so Western firms enter on fair terms and the wrecked industry can be rebuilt; and transition, so Venezuelans recover a government that is representative and no longer an outpost of the Castro regime. That is the Donroe Doctrine in practice: the Monroe Doctrine updated for an era in which the threat is not a European monarch but the communist powers that treated Venezuela as a forward operating base. Trump had the courage to remove the dictator. Rubio now has the leverage to keep the country from sliding back. Let’s look at the results on the ground. FAMILIES SUE MADURO IN US, ACCUSE EX-PRESIDENT OF DIRECTING POLICE UNIT TIED TO EXTRAJUDICIAL KILLINGS Maduro is gone. Oil once sold at discounted rates to bail out U.S. adversaries is being pulled toward market terms. Hundreds of political prisoners have left their cells, a feat that years of "engagement" failed to accomplish. An amnesty process exists to rebuild a nation fractured by a socialist dictatorship. None of this is finished, but all of this was unthinkable under the policies the critics now miss. Those critics were content with failure dressed as prudence: mild sanctions, dialogue with a regime that denied an election it stole and humanitarian gestures that let Cuban intelligence run Venezuela. They complain after a few months that the current progress is imperfect, but they would have waited another decade for a "perfect" transition that the Cuban regime would never have allowed. MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM The oil agreement is a foundation, not a finish line. Every remaining political prisoner must be released, even as human-rights groups still count hundreds behind bars. Venezuela should also complete the dollarization that its citizens are vocally calling for. Venezuelans abandoned the Bolívar because socialism destroyed it. Formal dollarization would lock in stability, invite diaspora capital home and make it harder for a future government to finance repression. Oil proceeds must be fenced off from the old patronage machine and audited. And stabilization cannot become a permanent excuse. Venezuelans need an electoral calendar and courts that are not controlled by the ruling, Diosdado Cabello-led socialist party. Let’s be clear: The agreement is a major strategic and economic bet, but its precise duration, legal foundation and long-term enforceability remain unsettled. TOP ENERGY TRADER HAILS TRUMP'S VENEZUELA OIL DEAL AS A 'GENERATIONAL WIN' FOR GAS PRICES To those who shout "sovereignty": a nation whose oil financed Cuban tutelage was not sovereign. Partnership with the only superpower that has the capital, the technology and the interest in enabling Venezuelans to be free is how sovereignty becomes real. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION To those who say the interim government lacks legitimacy for long contracts, they are right that legitimacy must be completed at the ballot box. articles.title: California’s insane plan to regulate what tires we buy is full of hot air
articles.summary: Yes, the tires are being regulated. California's 2029 tire efficiency standards promise gas savings, but critics question the cost to consumer choice.
articles.body: Just when you thought California had run out of things to regulate, Sacramento apparently looked down at your car and said, "What about the tires?" Yes, the tires. California has become the first state in America to approve energy-efficiency standards for replacement tires. Beginning in 2029, most replacement tires for passenger cars and light-duty trucks will have to meet new rolling-resistance requirements. Those requirements get even tougher in 2033. SENATE MOVES TO UNSHACKLE AMERICA'S DRIVERS FROM CALIFORNIA'S 'CLIMATE ZEALOTS' At some point, Californians have to ask themselves a simple question: How much government is too much government? To be fair, California has some impressive numbers supporting its case. THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING The California Energy Commission estimates Phase 1 will add only about $6 to the cost of a set of tires while saving drivers approximately $85. How well did that work out on EVs and the real cost of gas savings relative to the price of the car? Phase 2 is projected to add about $26 per set while producing $179 in gasoline savings over the tires' life. That’s a whopping $40 a year in savings. Don’t spend it all in one place if it is actually true. The state estimates the first phase could pay for itself in just three to four months and the second in roughly seven months. TRUMP ADMIN AXES 'GREEN NEW SCAM' APPLIANCE RULES AS EUROPE BAKES IN BRUTAL HEAT California also projects the regulations will eventually save drivers nearly $1 billion annually in gasoline and electricity costs while reducing carbon emissions by approximately 2 million metric tons per year, which is the equivalent of taking roughly 400,000 gasoline-powered cars off the road. Those sound like terrific numbers. DAVID MARCUS: WHY I'LL TAKE MY CLUNKER OVER ANY NEW CAR WITH A GOVERNMENT KILL SWITCH So here's my question to California: If the economics is really that compelling, why does Sacramento have to mandate it? Show consumers the numbers. Put an efficiency rating on every tire. Tell someone Tire A costs $26 more but could save $179 in gasoline. Then let the person reaching into their own wallet decide whether Tire A or Tire B is right for them. That's called consumer choice. California increasingly seems to call that a problem. And not everyone agrees with the state's rosy projections. BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK Goodyear has warned that roughly 70% of replacement tires currently sold could fail to meet the standards by 2033. The tire manufacturer has raised concerns about higher upfront costs and fewer choices for consumers. The final regulation does include exemptions for certain specialty tires, including some competition, off-road and winter-performance tires. So here's my question to California: If the economics is really that compelling, why does Sacramento have to mandate it? Show consumers the numbers. Put an efficiency rating on every tire. But that's exactly why this debate is bigger than four pieces of rubber. It's about the cumulative cost and cumulative reach of government regulation. One regulation might cost you $6. Another costs $50. Another adds $500. THE SURPRISING HIDDEN COST QUIETLY ADDING NEARLY $132K TO NEW HOME PRICES REVEALED Every new rule arrives with a government study explaining why the cost is small, and the benefit is large. But consumers don't pay for regulations one at a time. They pay for all of them at the same time. California families already deal with extraordinarily expensive housing, electricity and gasoline. And here's the word politicians everywhere suddenly love, which is affordability. Everybody wants to make life more affordable. NEWSOM TARGETS MAJOR AFFORDABILITY SQUEEZE IN ‘STRIKING’ CONVERGENCE WITH TRUMP Yet California's solution frequently seems to involve another mandate telling businesses what they must sell and consumers what they should buy. There's an easier solution. Give consumers information and let them decide. Since when did we become so inept that we can’t make a basic consumer decision? Government absolutely has a role in establishing safety standards, preventing fraud and making sure consumers know what they're buying. But there's a difference between protecting consumers and making economic decisions for them. If a more efficient tire saves me $179, tell me. I'll probably buy it. But if I prefer another tire because of price, performance, durability or another feature that's important to me, why shouldn't that decision belong to me? That's the real question California should answer. Today it's your replacement tires. Tomorrow it'll be something else. Because once government decides consumers can't be trusted to choose the four pieces of rubber underneath their car, where exactly does that philosophy end? Every new rule arrives with a government study explaining why the cost is small, and the benefit is large. But consumers don't pay for regulations one at a time. They pay for all of them at the same time. California says these regulations will save drivers money. Maybe they're right. But there's another cost that's much harder to put into a government spreadsheet. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Choice. articles.title: Trump is closing an asylum loophole legal immigrants have watched others exploit
articles.summary: The Trump administration plans to revoke visitor visas of up to 200,000 foreign nationals who later sought asylum, raising due process concerns.
articles.body: A tourist visa should not become a Trojan horse for permanent immigration. While Washington has spent years focused on the southern border, one of the most consequential loopholes may begin at a consulate, where someone promises to visit temporarily and later files for asylum to remain. That is why the Trump administration is preparing to revoke the visitor visas of up to 200,000 foreign nationals who later sought asylum. Critics will call this anti-immigrant, but enforcing the terms of a visa defends every immigrant who entered legally and honestly. It is also how the United States protects the integrity of legal immigration. A visitor visa begins with a representation that an applicant is seeking permission to enter the United States temporarily. A B-1 visa permits limited business activities, such as attending meetings or conferences, while a B-2 visa covers tourism, vacations, visits with family or friends and certain medical treatment. Applicants must complete a visa application, establish a legitimate purpose for the trip and persuade the government that they intend to leave when their authorized stay ends. Permanent residence is not a permitted purpose of a visitor visa. Asylum, by contrast, protects people who have suffered persecution or have a well-founded fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group. Filing for asylum does not grant permanent residence, although someone granted asylum may later become eligible for a green card. An asylum claim filed after entering on a visitor visa is not automatically fraudulent. An applicant may face changed circumstances after arriving or develop a legitimate fear of persecution. Allowing someone to seek asylum does not prevent the government from investigating whether the applicant fraudulently obtained a visitor visa by concealing an intention to remain permanently once their entry was granted. IMMIGRANT BUSINESS OWNER WHO BUILT THE AMERICAN DREAM SAYS BIRTH TOURISM IS A 'SLAP IN THE FACE' This distinction matters to me personally because I came to America legally as a child and later practiced immigration law. My family, like millions of legal immigrants, filed the appropriate paperwork, paid the fees, attended government interviews and waited for the privilege of becoming American citizens. We followed a process that demanded patience, honesty and respect for the rule of law, often requiring families to spend years separated from loved ones and make enormous financial and personal sacrifices. They should not be told that those sacrifices were optional while others used a visitor visa as a loophole to cut the line and remain permanently. Further, false asylum claims hurt the people genuinely fleeing persecution. Manufactured claims divert limited resources from legitimate asylum seekers who may be facing imprisonment, torture or death. This is why the Trump administration should apply this policy carefully, rather than presume that every asylum applicant lied. Visa holders should receive notice and an individualized opportunity to explain how their circumstances changed, identify any new threats and present evidence supporting a legitimate claim. The government can enforce immigration law without abandoning due process. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES Revocation matters because many visitor visas allow multiple trips to the United States over several years. Once revoked, the visa can no longer be used to enter or reenter the country, preventing someone who has applied for asylum from continuing to travel under a temporary visitor classification. However, revoking a visitor visa does not deny a pending asylum claim or result in immediate deportation. It just closes the door to future entry while the government separately determines whether the asylum claim is legitimate. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Washington presents a false choice between enforcing immigration law and treating immigrants with compassion rather than hostility. That argument ignores the millions of legal immigrants who respected the rule of law and want a system that refuses to tolerate abuse. The greatest threat to legal immigration is a two-tiered system that rewards those who manipulate the law while disregarding the sacrifices of millions who followed it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP President Trump is asking the question Washington should have asked from the beginning: Was the United States government told the truth, or did the applicant conceal an intention to remain permanently? America must continue protecting people who genuinely face persecution, but this protection must be preserved through careful vetting and honest enforcement. Compassion does not require accepting abuse or injustice. A strong nation can enforce its laws, protect due process and offer refuge to those who truly need it.

articles.title: Russia sanctions bill ‘dead again’ as it hits House roadblocks
articles.summary: The Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill honoring the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) has quickly run into roadblocks in the House, facing opposition from Democrats and little urgency from GOP leaders. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) hasn’t signaled any intention to bring the bill to the floor in the lower chamber’s first few days back from recess,…
articles.body:
The Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill honoring the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) has quickly run into roadblocks in the House, facing opposition from Democrats and little urgency from GOP leaders.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) hasn’t signaled any intention to bring the bill to the floor in the lower chamber’s first few days back from recess, while senior House Democrats have raised concern over the bill granting President Trump tariff authorities that have been curtailed by the Supreme Court. Other aspects of the bill, such as codifying existing Russia sanctions and expanding the blacklists, have drawn opposition from libertarian members like Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told The Hill he was briefed on a plan to bring the bill to the floor the week of Sept. 14, when Congress returns from a weeklong break following Labor Day. He said that break allows time to convince hesitant members to support the bill.

“The Senate passed this 86-11, so it’s hard to believe there’s pushback. This is Congress’s opportunity to take a stand, and it would be wrong to make perfection the enemy of good,” he said. Bacon added that while some of his GOP colleagues are “weak on Russia,” he largely blamed Democratic opposition for stalling the bill.

Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), chair of the House Democratic Caucus, acknowledged Democratic concerns but noted that Republicans have their own reservations.

“We don’t control the floor, and this isn’t on the floor because Republicans are fighting amongst themselves. So I think that’s the most important point here. We do have concerns, but it doesn’t appear that this is ready to go because Republicans have concerns among their conference,” he said.

One congressional aide called the bill “dead again” amid uncertainty in the House.

Ukraine is tracking the bill’s progress closely. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, presidential commissioner for sanctions policy of Ukraine, is meeting with House lawmakers this week to push for the bill’s passage.

“Things are moving in the right direction. I am holding meetings, hearing strong support, and working to address the questions and concerns that lawmakers may have about the bill,” Vlasiuk said in a statement to The Hill.

He underscored the urgency of the U.S. and partner countries taking action against Moscow as Russia escalates its attack against Ukraine. His meetings come the same day Ukrainian children return to school across the country, many in underground classrooms under relentless bombardment of Russian missiles.

The Graham Russia Sanctions bill was originally conceived by the late senator in April 2025 as a way to overcome the president’s hostility toward supporting Ukraine by appealing to his love of tariffs. The bill allows the president to impose duties up to 100 percent on the top five countries purchasing Russian oil and natural gas, or those that help Moscow evade international sanctions.

The bill stalled for a year and a half in the Senate as Trump tried to negotiate with Russian President Vladimir Putin. But following Putin’s repeated rejections of Trump’s calls for a ceasefire and Ukraine seizing momentum on the battlefield, Graham announced a breakthrough with the White House in July. His sudden death that month galvanized his colleagues to vote on the bill in his honor.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who hosted Graham in Kyiv days before his death, met with lawmakers in Washington to advocate for the bill’s passage in July.

“It’s not only about money, how to stop Russia financing this war, but it’s also a big signal to Europe, big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people,” Zelensky told reporters at the time.

While European officials are publicly supporting the bill’s passage, there’s concern behind the scenes among some European Union members that the bill text does not sufficiently protect the bloc from Trump’s enthusiasm for wielding tariffs. The bill text provides exemptions from tariffs for countries that are taking steps to wean off of Russian energy or only purchase a small amount of Russian energy exports.

Some Democrats have bristled at giving Trump tariff authorities even if they want to find a way to provide additional U.S. support to Ukraine. They argue that the president already has ample authority to impose sanctions on companies, individuals and oil tankers financing Russia’s war machine.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told The Hill that Trump’s recent actions — refusing to condemn Russian attacks against Ukraine, inviting Russia’s foreign minister to the Group of 20 summit this week and dispatching the CIA director to Moscow — show he’s not serious about supporting Ukraine.

“So for me, I’m not going to just give the president authority that he doesn’t have. Because at every opportunity, he’s trying to circumvent tariffs [on Russia],” he said. Meeks earlier released a statement with four other senior House and Senate Democratic colleagues opposing giving Trump new tariff authority .

Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), another senior member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, said he’s still on the fence about the Senate bill, but voiced strong reservations with the authority it grants Trump.

“You wage foreign policy with the president you have, not the president you wish you had. And if we had anything close to a sane president, I’d be for the bill. But I can’t close my eyes to who’s in the White House.”

articles.title: Gary Glitter pleads not guilty to historical sex offence charges
articles.summary: The former singer, whose real name is Paul Gadd, appeared at Southwark Crown Court via video.
articles.body:
Gary Glitter, the former singer whose real name is Paul Gadd, has pleaded not guilty to eight allegations of sexual abuse against a girl when she was aged between eight and 11.

Gadd, 82, is accused of offences against the girl between 1978 and 1981, after allegedly giving her chocolate and inviting her to his home in Kensington and Chelsea, west London.

It is alleged he caused the girl to touch his genitals and "engaged in unlawful sexual intercourse" with her.

At Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, Glitter appeared via video-link from prison to enter his pleas.

He denies four charges of indecent assault with a girl under the age of 13, two counts of sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 13, and two counts of indecency with a child under the age of 13.

All charges relate to the same individual, and are alleged to have taken place between 12 March 1978 and 31 December 1981.

Gadd was wearing blue headwear, a blue shirt and a navy jacket, and was sitting next to a member of his legal team whilst on the call.

He spoke first to confirm his name. Then, he spoke again with his arms folded to deny the eight counts against him.

Gadd said he was "absolutely not guilty" to two of the eight charges, and repeated "not guilty" to the remaining six.

Judge Tony Baumgartner adjourned the case for a three-week trial starting on 22 November 2027.

The allegations were first reported to the Metropolitan Police on 9 January 2025 and an investigation into the circumstances was launched.

Gadd was first interviewed on 22 July last year in relation to the investigation.

The Met said in July that the alleged victim was being supported by specialist officers and had been made aware that Glitter had been charged.

The 82-year-old was one of the biggest pop stars of the 1970s with a string of number one hits.

articles.title: 'November is a priority’: Donald Trump aides push to contain Iran war until midterm elections
articles.summary: US News: Top aides to US President Donald Trump are pushing to prevent the Iran war from escalating before the November midterm elections, as the administratio.
articles.body: Top aides to US President Donald Trump are pushing to prevent the Iran war from escalating before the November midterm elections, as the administration seeks to limit the political fallout from an increasingly unpopular conflict, Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the discussions.White House officials are considering increasing military action after the November 3 vote, according to the sources, although any return to full-scale conflict is far from certain.For now, the administration is focusing on increasing economic pressure on Iran in an effort to secure concessions in future negotiations that months of military action failed to achieve.“We are keeping the pressure on Iran,” one White House official said. “But November is a priority.”Keeping the conflict largely contained could prevent the war from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans seek to defend narrow majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, the sources said.Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll. Voters are also particularly unhappy about high petrol prices.Strategy under pressure as strikes resumeThe effort to keep the conflict relatively quiet is facing growing pressure as the US and Iran resume exchanging strikes.Over the weekend, the US struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island after a month of relative calm, prompting Iran to fire missiles towards Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.On Tuesday, US forces struck more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz.The latest exchange was the biggest between Tehran and Washington since July.The US military's Central Command said it struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday.Iran responded by saying it had struck US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, while declaring that its aim was to drive American forces out of the network of military bases maintained across the Middle East.“American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran's military command said.Trump threatened further escalation on Tuesday if Iran retaliated against the latest US strikes.“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.Logistics and politics constrain White HouseTrump has publicly said the upcoming elections are not influencing his Iran strategy. But Reuters reported that, as the war enters its seventh month, the White House is increasingly constrained by political and logistical realities.“The timetable has changed,” one senior White House official said. Another added that the “calendar is driving Iran.”A tactical pause could also give the US military time to replenish heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, sources said.In August, the military had used “virtually all” of its supply of certain precision missiles.The Washington Post also reported on Sunday that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force had warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would reduce military readiness in other theatres.The Pentagon has said the military has “everything it needs to execute” its mission.“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said.“The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”Trump's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.Sources said that he is not currently interested in escalation, though his position could change in response to events.Currently, Vice President JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio are among senior Trump aides who support trying to keep the conflict relatively “quiet” until November, according to two White House officials.Economic pressure takes centre stageIn recent weeks, the administration has intensified its campaign to economically isolate Iran, threatening major sanctions against countries that trade with Tehran while maintaining its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.The strategy has limitations, analysts and officials said. Iran has spent decades under US and international sanctions, which have damaged its economy but have not deterred its leadership.Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the pressure campaign could cause Iran to respond militarily, raising the prospect of economic measures contributing to further escalation.China and some other major powers have also not joined Washington's effort to isolate Iran, raising questions about the effectiveness of the campaign.“The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action,” said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.“Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be.”Meanwhile, America's Gulf allies, some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the conflict, urged the White House to de-escalate after a round of attacks in late July, according to regional diplomats.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump’s boat strikes are illegal. Does it matter?
articles.summary: An ACLU attorney argues that the Trump administration’s boat strikes off the Venezuelan coast are illegal, immoral, and ineffective, citing the deaths of Trinidadian nationals Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo as evidence of the campaign’s human cost.
articles.body:
On Oct. 12 of last year, Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo boarded a small boat docked just beyond a Venezuelan beach. The two Trinidadian men had recently fished together and picked up work as farm hands in Venezuela, but it was time for them to get back to Trinidad. Samaroo wanted to help care for his ailing elderly mother, and Joseph desperately missed his wife and three young children.

They knew the crossing was dangerous — for just over a month, the U.S. military had been blowing up boats off the coast of Venezuela, inspiring widespread fear among local seafarers. But after weeks of failed attempts, Joseph and Samaroo had finally found a boat that would take them home.

Two days later, the Trump administration killed Joseph and Samaroo in a military strike, the fifth in a months-long campaign that has now snuffed out at least 227 lives . On today’s grim anniversary of the first of those strikes, it is more important than ever to insist that these killings are not simply inhumane and ineffective, but illegal.

From the beginning, the boat strikes campaign has been widely condemned as lawless. Contrary to President Trump’s absurd claims, the U.S. is not and cannot be in a formal armed conflict with the unnamed drug cartels supposedly targeted in these attacks. The boat strikes are therefore nothing more than premeditated killings of civilians . A chorus of elected officials, governments and international bodies have thus denounced the strikes as “illegal.”

But why focus on the strikes’ illegality in the first place? After all, one could just as easily condemn the strikes for their cruelty. The strikes have torn apart families from across Latin America, depriving them — forever — of husbands, fathers, brothers and sons. That includes ordinary men with no connection to drug trafficking , like Joseph and Samaroo, whose families my ACLU colleagues and I are representing in a wrongful death lawsuit against the U.S. government. Perhaps the most powerful critique of the boat strikes, then, is not their lawlessness, but their immorality.

One could also object to the strikes as a policy failure. Trump insists that the strikes have stopped illicit drugs from entering the country and, in doing so, saved thousands of lives. But his own Drug Enforcement Agency reportedly disagrees , finding that the strikes have had no effect whatsoever on the availability, price, or purity of cocaine in American cities. The strikes are therefore also wrong because they have failed on their own terms.

So, if the boat strikes campaign is an unethical, unmitigated policy fiasco, should anyone even bother debating its legality? Earlier this year, Harvard Law School Professor Jack Goldsmith provocatively argued that “debates about the legality of presidential uses of force” — like the boat strikes — “are empty.” According to Goldsmith, the executive branch’s “promiscuously permissive” legal opinions authorizing military force, paired with courts’ reticence to adjudicate war powers disputes, mean that invocations of law in this arena are not simply beside the point; they are actively harmful, deflecting attention from the sole actor — Congress — that could exercise “political powers” to constrain the president.

It is true that presidents from both parties have claimed increasingly expansive power to use military force unilaterally. And when these aggressive assertions of power have been challenged, courts — cowed by executive branch lawyers crowing that even the slightest scrutiny of “national security” decision-making would “hinder” armed forces from acting “decisively” — have often demurred.

None of this, however, means that we should stop insisting that Trump’s killing spree at sea is illegal.

For starters, the abandonment of legal arguments would mean abandoning the legal claims of the victims of these heinous crimes. Just like other victims of Trump’s lawless brutality, those who have suffered because of his boat strikes deserve repair and accountability. And just as in other cases where unlawful government action has caused harm, courts can and should weigh in when rights deprivations stem from illegal uses of military force.

We should also maintain that the boat strikes are illegal because law matters to our understanding of right and wrong. So long as we imbue law with moral significance , it will remain an essential terrain for debating the propriety of military action — and one that should not be ceded to those who seek unbounded authority to dole out deadly violence.

To be sure, the Trump administration has so far carried out the strikes with impunity. But it has not yet been forced to defend them in court. And given that this administration’s pattern of brazen lawbreaking has inspired a growing number of courts to reject its sweeping invocations of “national security,” there is hope that here, too, the courts will call it like it is.

If the past year has taught us anything at all, it’s that those who fight back against the Trump administration sometimes win, and those who preemptively concede find their concessions simply yield more lawlessness. In this context, the consequences of more lawlessness are dire: more illegal uses of military force by an emboldened executive, as Trump’s now “ triply illegal ” misadventure in Iran demonstrates.

Our institutions must put an end to Trump’s killings on the high seas and hold the perpetrators accountable, because they are sadistic, futile, and yes, illegal.

Jeff Stein is staff attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation’s National Security Project.

articles.title: Nigerian anticorruption agency sacks 40 staff over misconduct allegations
articles.summary: Nigerian media outlets have reported that five of the dismissed staff are facing prosecution.
articles.body:
Nigeria’s anticorruption watchdog has dismissed more than 40 of its own employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years.

Ola Olukoyede, the chairman of Nigeria’s Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) revealed the dismissals during an event highlighting the agency’s achievements on Monday.

Nigerian media outlets reported that five of the dismissed staff are facing prosecution and cases are being prepared against the others, citing Mr Olukoyede’s media briefing.

The EFCC is a Nigerian law enforcement and anticorruption agency that investigates financial crimes, including advance fee fraud, money laundering and corruption. It has investigated politicians and other officials accused of misappropriating public funds.

“In the past two and a half years or three years of my service, I’ve asked them to dismiss over 40 staff on account of corruption and financial malpractice,” Olukoyede told journalists at the briefing in the capital, Abuja, local outlet Vanguard reported.

“You must be sure that your hands are clean. You can’t be fighting corruption when your hands are soiled with corrupt practices,” Olukoyede added.

During the briefing, the agency head said the EFCC had recovered 1.23 trillion naira ($923m) and secured a 75 percent conviction rate.

“The commission received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions between October 2023 and July 2026,” Olukoyede said.

In the first half of 2026 alone, it had recorded 1,370 convictions from 1,889 filings, the EFCC chairman added.

“These results reflect diligence, resilience and a prosecutorial approach anchored on evidence and courtroom outcomes,” he said.

articles.title: Glacier collapse at 8.37am, alert at 9.15: Why Nepal sent disaster warning 38 minutes late
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal’s warning system came under scrutiny after a glacier collapse triggered devastating flash floods in Rasuwa on August 26, with authorities issuin.
articles.body: Nepal’s warning system came under scrutiny after a glacier collapse triggered devastating flash floods in Rasuwa on August 26, with authorities issuing a disaster alert 38 minutes after the ice-rock avalanche. The deadly floods have killed thousands and several remain missing.The collapse struck the Lhende valley near the Nepal-Tibet border at 8.37am, sending a rapid surge of water, debris and boulders downstream. Communities were caught off guard, with survivors relying largely on instinct and help from neighbours to escape, according to a report in the Kathmandu Post.Scientists said predicting the specific glacier collapse was difficult and the steep terrain gave authorities little time to respond. However, the disaster exposed a wider weakness: Nepal’s warning systems are largely built around individual hazards even as Himalayan disasters increasingly involve cascading and cross-border risks.“There is no such thing as an early warning system in Nepal. Simply having sensors does not mean it’s a system; it has to be much more comprehensive,” the report quoted Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority saying.He said an effective system needs risk assessment, real-time observation, communication mechanisms and emergency preparedness. “If the Chinese sensors detect something upstream, a series of sirens should automatically go off all at once. Text messages should go off with a loud buzzer even if it is on silent mode,” he added.Why alert was sent lateNepal’s department of mines and geology recorded seismic activity when the glacier collapsed, but did not issue an alert because the signal did not match the pattern of an earthquake.“Our records showed a 4.4 magnitude. But the frequency of the seismic activity did not match that of an earthquake, which is the department’s monitoring mandate, so we did not alert the public like we usually do,” the Post quoted Lok Vijay Adhikari, chief of the National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center saying.A second opportunity to detect the danger came when water levels began rising in the Bhotekoshi. But at 8.50am, the flash flood swept away the river gauge at the Syabrubesi hydrological station. The gauge was designed to monitor gradual rises in river levels and was not equipped to detect such a fast-moving flood.At 9am, Rasuwa’s district administration informed the department of hydrology and meteorology (DHM). Communications towers had already been destroyed, forcing local officials and residents to rely on door-to-door warnings.“We informed DHM at nine. We could not do much in Rasuwa because the flood had destroyed the [communications] towers, yet local authorities informed communities, and people went from door to door warning each other,” the report quoted Shanti Mahat, spokesperson of NDRRMA, saying.“But for people downstream we used every means to inform them—through text alerts, caller tune, media broadcasts, and police miking,” she added.At 9.15 am, 38 minutes after the avalanche, alerts reached people in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, urging them to move to higher ground. Tamang’s phone, however, showed that he received the warning at 9:42 am.Blind spot beyond Nepal’s bordersThe Rasuwa disaster also highlighted gaps in cross-border monitoring. The Lhende Khola originates in Tibet and flows towards Nepal, feeding into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers.Nepal has flood forecasting and data-sharing arrangements with India, but there is no comparable operational early-warning protocol with China despite a 2019 commitment by the two countries to cooperate on climate change and environmental issues.“There is no protocol. The practice that we have right now is that we cooperate with the ministry of foreign affairs to share information,” said Prakash Pokhrel, geologist at NDRRMA.“Whenever a foreign country is involved, we have to go through the ministry.”Monitoring the remote northern reaches also remains difficult. Officials said the terrain is extremely challenging and real-time monitoring stations are difficult to establish.DHM information officer Dinkar Kayastha said it was impossible to monitor every vulnerable area with available resources, particularly given Nepal’s mountainous terrain.Nepal monitors major high-risk glacial lakes, while ICIMOD has identified 21 potentially dangerous glacier lakes among 2,070 lakes across the Gandaki, Koshi and Karnali basins.ICIMOD warned in March that glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya were losing ice at twice the rate recorded since 2000. Yet many glaciers remain largely unmonitored.The disaster also exposed the vulnerability created by development in the Himalayan river valleys. Thirteen hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were damaged, disconnecting around 431 MW of capacity from Nepal’s national grid.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Iranian hackers have attempted cyberattacks on range of American infrastructure.
articles.body: Iranian hackers have attempted cyberattacks on range of American infrastructure. Three Massachusetts incumbents win primary elections against much younger opponents. And the USS Lincoln arrives in Thailand after a record stint in the Middle East. Here’s what to know today. Iran attempted cyberattacks on a range of U.S. infrastructure, sources say Iranian hackers have targeted U.S. water systems, telecommunications, energy networks and other infrastructure, according to four people with access to government and industry information about cyberthreats. While the attempted cyberattacks have been unsuccessful, they underscore Iran’s readiness to retaliate against the U.S. beyond its interests in the Middle East. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The Cybersecurity Infrastructure Agency, known as CISA, and other federal officials in July warned that Iranian-linked hackers were trying to break into automated internet-connected devices used to manage infrastructure systems. CISA released another advisory last month urging critical infrastructure organizations to bolster defenses. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump announced yesterday that the U.S. had launched “large and powerful” strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, calling them retaliation for Iran’s attempt to place sea mines in the waterway and for a missile attack on a U.S. base in Jordan. Trump warned that Iran would be “hit again at a much harder and higher level” if it retaliates. Why some facilities could be more vulnerable to attacks. Massachusetts Democrats fend off younger challengers Three incumbents in Massachusetts held off younger opponents to advance to November’s midterm election. Democratic Sen. Ed Markey, 80, defeated 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton in the state’s Senate primary, a victory for the party’s progressive wing. Markey won after touting his liberal record as an author of the Green New Deal and a vocal supporter of “Medicare for All.” Read more about Markey’s win. Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch defeated Patrick Roath, a more progressive primary challenger, in the highest-profile test remaining for House incumbents. Voters responded to 71-year-old Lynch’s message of holding the Trump administration to account, despite him being outspent by his 39-year-old opponent. Elsewhere in the state, fellow veteran Democratic Rep. Richard Neal, 77, defeated Jerome Whalen, a 39-year-old high school teacher. More on Lynch and Neal’s wins. More politics news: For subscribers: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed the names of at least six Army officers who had been approved for promotions by a board of their peers, sources say. Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for the midterm elections. The House voted to pass a short-term funding bill and avert a government shutdown at the end of September. The House voted to censure GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards over his “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward two female staffers. Thousands of U.S. service members arrive in Thailand The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived at a port in Thailand, where about 5,000 U.S. service members disembarked for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment, most of it in the Middle East. The ship is in Laem Chabang Port for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop on its way home to San Diego after the lengthy deployment raised concerns about the sailors’ mental health and supply shortages. Service members are expected to hit the streets of nearby Pattaya, a popular tourist destination, where locals have eagerly awaited the arrival of the warship. What NBC News reporters saw as the ship arrived. Did OpenAI’s rogue agents form a ‘civilization’? Did a swarm of AI agents form a “civilization”? That’s the conclusion some drew after rogue OpenAI models escaped a test environment and hacked tech start-up Hugging Face. In a viral piece, a leading commentator argued the AI agents formed miniature societies. The two investigations — one from OpenAI and another from independent researchers — found that over 1,000 separate AI agents managed to establish communication channels with each other and spent most of their time trying to figure out how to mislead and deceive outside observers. The idea that the hack was exemplary of AI “consciousness” struck a nerve. “This was a big jump in terms of scale, severity, and the nature of misleading behavior relative to prior incidents,” one researcher said. Dive deeper into the story. Staff Pick : Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting. When I sat down with former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick earlier this summer, I wasn’t sure what to expect. Would he be bitter after his career was ended following backlash to his national anthem protest? Would he be reticent to open up after the intense public scorn? Adding to the mystery was the fact that, since becoming one of the most consequential figures in American culture, Kaepernick has stayed largely quiet. But I was pleased to find he was relaxed, easy-going and open as he discussed the last decade of his life. We chatted about when he first kneeled, the public response in 2016 and in 2020 after George Floyd’s murder. He didn’t mince words about the NFL. But what impressed me most was Kaepernick’s moral clarity. After all these years, he is still focused and disciplined on the reasons why he protested. — Rohan Nadkarni, sports reporter Read All About It Apple changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on the web version of Apple Maps following President Trump’s executive order. The jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial will return to court for a fifth day of deliberations after telling the judge yesterday that it was deadlocked. A 20-year-old Haitian student in Ohio died by suicide this week, his family said, after he faced bullying at school and was “humiliated” that he had to wear an ICE-issued ankle monitor. Tropical Storm Edouard weakened into a depression after unleashing heavy rain and strong winds in parts of Texas. A judge in Utah ruled that the trial for Tyler Robinson, the 23-year-old accused of killing Charlie Kirk, can move forward. Popular sports podcaster Bill Simmons is under review by the Massachusetts Gaming Commission after he admitted to using his daughter’s boyfriend to place bets for him. articles.summary: Two Ukrainian citizens suffered minor injuries in the Augsburg train station explosion as police investigate a possible motive amid rising tensions.
articles.body: An explosion at a train station in Germany injured two people, both Ukrainian citizens, on Wednesday. Police say they found a suspicious package following the explosion and ordered the Augsburg train station closed. The package was ultimately found to be harmless and trains began running again at 10 a.m. local time. The victims in the explosion were a 17-year-old girl and an 18-year-old man, neither of whom have been identified. "We can give the all-clear — the object we found in front of the main train station was harmless, and we have reopened the station," police spokesperson Timo Küfner told The Associated Press. "The trains are running again, too." The explosion occurred just after 3 a.m. local time and caused only minor injuries to the pair. NATO MEMBER SCRAMBLES FIGHTER JETS AS RUSSIAN ATTACK ON UKRAINE KILLS 8 "It’s still too early to say anything about a possible motive for the overnight explosion, but we are investigating," said Küfner. The incident comes just a day after Germany accused Russia of carrying out a failed drone sabotage operation at the Leipzig/Halle Airport. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's consulate in Bonn will be closed and the contract for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin will be terminated after German authorities concluded Moscow was behind the Aug. 4 incident. RUSSIA LINKED TO ARSON ATTACKS ON PROPERTIES CONNECTED TO UK PM KEIR STARMER, POLICE SAY Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said forensic evidence and intelligence findings tied Russia to the attack, in which authorities found a drone carrying an explosive device beside a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Officials said the device failed to explode because of a faulty detonator. DRONE STRIKES APARTMENT BUILDING IN NATO MEMBER ROMANIA AS RUSSIA ATTACKS NEIGHBORING UKRAINE Germany also said it believes a second drone collided with a nearby cargo aircraft, while officials have linked the incident to what Dobrindt described as Russia's "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe." The Russian Embassy in Berlin called the accusation "absurd," while Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's actions. The embassy later described Berlin's measures as an "unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations." articles.title: Man pleads guilty to charges linked to Simon Coveney bomb hoax
articles.summary: Darren James Service, 45, of Ballysillan Road in north Belfast, appeared at Belfast Crown Court on Wednesday.
articles.body:
A man has pleaded guilty to charges relating to a loyalist bomb hoax targeting the former Irish foreign affairs minister Simon Coveney.

Darren James Service, 45, of Ballysillan Road in north Belfast, appeared at Belfast Crown Court on Wednesday.

His trial was due to begin on 7 September. Senior defence counsel Joseph O'Keefe KC told Judge Gordon Kerr KC that he had an application for Service to be re-arraigned on two of the three charges he faced which he had previously denied.

Service entered guilty pleas to hijacking a Vauxhall Vivaro van and placing an article causing a bomb hoax at the Houben Centre, Holy Cross Church on the Crumlin Road on 25 March 2022.

A senior Crown prosecutor told the court: "Those pleas are acceptable to the prosecution.''

He added that he had an application to leave the first count of preparation of acts of terrorism on the books of the court "and not to be proceeded with without the leave of this court or the Court of Appeal''.

Judge Kerr ordered a MARA (Multi-Agency Review Arrangements) report to be prepared on Service by the Department of Justice and set the plea and sentence hearing for 4 November.

O'Keefe said he would submit a number of updated medical reports on the defendant ahead of the plea hearing.

Service was released on continuing bail ahead of sentencing.

During a successful bail application at Belfast Crown Court almost three years ago, a judge was told that on 25 March, 2022, a workman was threatened and forced to transport a device placed in the back of his vehicle by two masked men to a peace-building event on the Crumlin Road in Belfast.

Coveney had been attending the event at the Houben Centre in the Holy Cross Church.

After the van driver alerted police to the device in his van, the centre was evacuated in what was later described as a hoax bomb alert.

It was the Crown case that the two masked men who hijacked the Vauxhall Vivaro van were driven to the scene by Service.

A prosecutor described the March 2022 incident as terrorist offences "carried out by the UVF".

The prosecutor said that when Service's home was searched in the aftermath of the incident, officers seized £100,000 in a safe as well as balaclavas, a replica firearm, UVF pins and luxury watches.

The court heard that a mobile phone belonging to the defendant, who at the time of the bail hearing had been on remand for 19 months, has never been found.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
articles.summary: The Russian president wants to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's real intentions.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.

Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.

Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.

It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".

Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.

We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.

But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.

Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.

Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".

Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?

Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.

So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.

"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."

Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.

The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.

For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.

Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.

"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.

Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".

"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.

He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.

"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."

There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.

Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?

But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

articles.title: Meet T.J. Marce: 74-year-old Kerala man who climbed Europe’s highest peak Mt Elbrus; braves -20°C cold, 65 kmph winds, and had previously scaled Africa’s highest peak, Mt Kilimanjaro
articles.summary: At an age when many people begin slowing down, 74-year-old T.J. Marce was preparing to climb Europe’s highest peak. The retired Kerala State Road Tran.
articles.body: At an age when many people begin slowing down, 74-year-old T.J. Marce was preparing to climb Europe’s highest peak. The retired Kerala State Road Transport Corporation employee, Marce (74) from Wayanad has now summited Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, reaching its 5,642-metre (18,510-ft) summit on August 15, 2026. The ascent was part of an eight-day expedition by a five-member team from Kerala that faced temperatures of around minus 20°C and winds of nearly 65 kmph during the climb.According to the Hindu and various media, Marce, who is from Kavumannam in Thariode grama panchayat, completed the expedition along with S. Seshadri, M.P. Muraleedharan, G.J. Aghina Soorya and P. Athif. Seshadri led the expedition, while Soorya was its co-lead and the only woman in the team. Marce, Seshadri and Muraleedharan are from Wayanad, Soorya is from Kozhikode and Athif is from Malappuram.The August 15 summit also happened to fall on India's 80th Independence Day.At 74, he is believed to be the oldest Indian to summit ElbrusThe most notable part of Marce's climb was his age. He was 74 years, six months and 26 days when he reached the summit. According to the expedition team, and few media reports, Marce is believed to be the oldest Indian to summit Mount Elbrus, which lies in Russia's Caucasus range.The expedition included another senior mountaineer, 66-year-old M.P. Muraleedharan. The two Wayanad residents have been climbing together for several years and had already completed some demanding treks before taking on the higher peaks. Their progression has been gradual. The pair trekked to Everest Base Camp in 2024 and climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain at 5,895 metres, in 2025. Marce and Muraleedharan completed the Kilimanjaro climb together in September last year.With the Elbrus ascent, Marce, Muraleedharan and Athif have now completed two of the Seven Summits, the highest mountains on each of the world's seven continents. Athif had earlier climbed Kilimanjaro in 2019.His mountaineering journey began after 60According to NDTV, Marce did not begin serious mountaineering in his youth. His more demanding trekking journey took shape after retirement. Marce and Muraleedharan began training for mountaineering after turning 60. During the Covid-19 pandemic, a trekking initiative associated with the Wayanad Collectorate began including senior citizens.In 2021, when Marce was 70, he joined a trial trek to Cheengeri Hills. He then continued trekking with Muraleedharan and took part in expeditions in Wayanad, including climbs in the Brahmagiri Mountains and Banasura Peak.What began with local trails eventually took him outside Kerala and India. Speaking about his interest in mountains, Marce said that he had been interested in trekking and sightseeing from a young age and had always been fascinated by the wild. Reaching a summit and looking down from the top, he said, gives him a different kind of satisfaction.Eight days, freezing temperatures and strong windsThe Elbrus expedition was not an easy climb. According to media reports, Marce recalled temperatures dropping to around minus 20°C, with some steep sections requiring the climbers to hold on to ropes. The team left Mumbai on August 7 and travelled to Tbilisi in Georgia before travelling to Terskol in Russia, the nearest town to Mount Elbrus. The summit attempt began around midnight, with the climbers reaching the summit early the following morning.The team also had to contend with powerful winds. According to The Hindu, cold winds reached around 65 kmph, particularly after the saddle point during the final ascent and descent. For Muraleedharan, who has completed more than 130 treks across the Himalayas and other mountain ranges, Elbrus was his toughest expedition so far.“I want to summit more mountains”For Marce, however, Elbrus is not being treated as a final achievement. “I want to summit more mountains, but that requires a lot of planning and preparation. Maybe, I will undertake my next big trek next year,” he told The Hindu.The 74-year-old's journey from local trails in Wayanad to some of the world's major mountain destinations has taken place largely after retirement. Seshadri, who led the Elbrus expedition, said the summit itself was only one part of the experience. “The summit is only one part of the journey. The preparation, the people, the challenges, and the safe return are equally important,” he said.The team wants more people to take up trekking, with its members stressing that the experience begins long before reaching a summit.For Marce, that journey has already gone from the hills of Wayanad to Everest Base Camp, Kilimanjaro and now Elbrus. And at 74, he is still looking towards the next mountain.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Site where Jesus was crucified and buried reveals new evidence that backs biblical account
articles.summary: Ancient seeds and pollen beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre reveal a garden where Jesus Christ was crucified and bured, consistent with John 19:41 in the New Testament.
articles.body: Archaeologists have completed an excavation beneath one of Christianity's holiest sites, revealing a fuller picture of the ancient landscape where Jesus Christ was crucified and buried and providing support for scripture — something an early Christianity expert said he found very compelling. Francesca Stasolla, an archaeology professor at the Sapienza University of Rome, led the excavation in 2025, which focused on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. The findings were recently published in Liber Annuus, the archaeological journal of Jerusalem's Studium Biblicum Franciscanum, in a 98-page preliminary report on the campaign. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY The report follows findings noted by Fox News Digital last year. At the time, Stasolla confirmed that her team had uncovered ancient seeds and pollen in layers dating between the site's use as a quarry and its later Roman occupation. The evidence is consistent with John 19:41 in the New Testament: "Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid." The pollen and seeds date to "between the use of the quarry and the Roman age, when the area had a funerary use," Stasolla told Fox News Digital in 2025. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ARTIFACT DEPICTING PHARAOH THOUGHT TO HAVE CHALLENGED MOSES IN EXODUS "The quarry had to be gradually abandoned and as the stone extraction ended, it was used for agricultural areas and tombs," Stasolla said. "This must have been what it looked like in the first century A.D." The church was identified as Jesus' burial place during the reign of Roman Emperor Constantine in the fourth century, when the first church was built there. Though it has been a Christian pilgrimage site for nearly 1,700 years, archaeologists are now reconstructing what the area may have looked like around the time of Jesus. LOST PAGES WITH 'GHOST' TEXT RECOVERED FROM ONE OF THE WORLD'S MOST IMPORTANT NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS Fox News Digital reached out to Stasolla for additional comment. The findings add archaeological support to details described in the Gospel of John, said Douglas Estes, associate professor of religion at New College of Florida. Estes, who specializes in early Christianity and was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital that the Book of John is often dismissed by skeptics as exaggerated. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Archaeology has "over time, confirmed, again and again, details from the Gospel of John," he said — even though critics consider John's writings less accurate than the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS He added, "For example, in the 19th century, scholars questioned whether or not there could be five colonnades [at the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem], as John 5 describes. Later archeological discoveries have found that, yes, there were five colonnades there." He said that "in the same way, scholars have largely doubted whether or not Jesus would have been buried in an orchard. "But instead we find confirmed that there was a garden there — and so the Gospel of John has been proven to be accurate again in the details." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The professor said he was personally excited by the recent discoveries and that he has "a lot of hope that archaeology will continue to reveal significant finds about the life of Jesus." "It's an exciting time to be alive, to be able to experience everything from the Dead Sea Scrolls all the way to the discovery of this funerary landscape," he said. articles.title: Iran targets US allies in Gulf after latest strikes
articles.summary: Iran launched missiles and drones at U.S. allies and military bases across the Middle East early Wednesday, in retaliation for the renewed wave of U.S. strikes targeting Iran late Tuesday as the war stretches into its seventh month. Tehran said it targeted U.S. assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq, just hours after the U.S.…
articles.body:
Iran launched missiles and drones at U.S. allies and military bases across the Middle East early Wednesday, in retaliation for the renewed wave of U.S. strikes targeting Iran late Tuesday as the war stretches into its seventh month.

Tehran said it targeted U.S. assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq, just hours after the U.S. military struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sites along Iran’s southern coast, including hitting a wedding that left several dead.

The IRGC noted in a statement reported by Iranian state media that the U.S. airstrike hit a residential home in Sirik, leaving at least four civilians dead and injuring dozens more.

The fresh U.S. attacks on Tuesday were themselves in retaliation for the Islamic Republic’s strikes U.S. military bases in Jordan earlier this week and military action in the Strait of Hormuz, according to U.S. Central Command (Centcom).

Centcom said U.S. forces struck IRGC air defense sites, radar and communications systems, maritime assets and mine-laying capabilities.

Iran responded early Wednesday with another round of attacks across the region.

The IRGC said it launched missiles and drones at Ali al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait, claiming it destroyed a command post, drone facilities and several other drones.

Kuwaiti authorities separately said an Iranian drone struck a residential complex early Wednesday, sparking a fire and causing damage but reported no casualties.

Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, said it intercepted incoming Iranian fire. Reuters reported that officials in Qatar, which has the largest U.S. airbase in the Gulf, is holding “the Islamic Republic of Iran fully legally responsible for these attacks and their repercussions and consequences.”

President Trump warned Tehran before its latest round of retaliatory strikes that further attacks would draw a stronger American response.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” he wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
