articles.title: Judge dismisses lawsuit against Lizzo's production company
articles.summary: The About Damn Time singer says she is "relieved" at the outcome and will "continue to fight" every claim.
articles.body:
US pop star Lizzo has spoken out after the remaining claims in a lawsuit against her production company were thrown out by a US district judge.

The singer's former wardrobe assistant Asha Daniels alleged she had been subjected to "degradation, forced physical labor, denial of medical care, sexual harassment, and racial harassment" while briefly working for Big Grrrl Big Touring in 2023.

District judge Fernando L Aenlle-Rocha filed a ruling to dismiss the claims by the stylist on Tuesday, according to court documents.

In an Instagram post , Lizzo said she was "relieved" at the outcome and will "continue to fight" every claim made against her and her company.

In 2024, judge Aenlle-Rocha ruled that Daniels could not sue the Grammy winner as an individual, but Big Grrrl Big Touring Inc remained a defendant.

In his ruling this week, he said the former wardrobe assistant did not identify any conduct by company employees that would demonstrate "general hostility to women in the workplace" or "disparate treatment of men and women".

He also wrote that this alleged conduct and these alleged incidents, "while inappropriate and unprofessional", fell "within the scope of what the Supreme Court has held to be outside the protection" of the "ordinary tribulations of the workplace".

Aenlle-Rocha also responded to an incident in which the stylist claims her foot was run over by a heavy clothes rack.

He wrote that while the court "does not seek to minimise or disregard the pain" felt, the injuries "do not qualify as disabilities" under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Following the ruling, the About Damn Time singer, whose real name is Melissa Viviane Jefferson, thanked her lawyers in her Instagram post.

"The truth matters to me more than anything and told y'all I will not settle and will continue to fight every vicious claim that has been made against me and my businesses," she added.

She also wrote that she will continue to use her platform to "spread positivity and light to the world" before signing off by sending love to her supporters.

Daniels' lawsuit, which was filed in September 2023, followed a separate suit filed by three of Lizzo's former tour dancers.

Those claims - which included sexual harassment - are denied by Lizzo's team.

Allegations of fat-shaming from the same lawsuit were dismissed by a judge in 2025.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Lizzo's and Daniels' lawyers for comment.

articles.title: Raging inferno erupts at Bali beachside restaurant party
articles.summary: Video shows flames engulfing a restaurant in Bali, Indonesia, after a reported balloon explosion during a birthday party sparked a massive inferno.
articles.body: A beachside party in Bali, Indonesia, erupted into chaos after a balloon reportedly exploded inside a popular restaurant, sparking a raging inferno. Videos captured flames ripping through the Chez Gado-Gado restaurant in the Seminyak resort area during the incident Sunday, which left an Australian teenager hospitalized with burns, according to 7News. "There was a 70th birthday, and they had two balloons on their table and a waitress went to light the candle on the birthday cake, but she lit it a bit too close to the balloon," Tara Borelli, a witness from Sydney, told News.com.au. "It popped, then exploded. We felt the heat from the pop." "I just grabbed my daughter and little cousin and ran straight onto the beach towards the water," Borelli added, describing how the straw roof of the restaurant immediately caught fire and "within minutes" the entire restaurant was ablaze. ONE TOURIST DEAD AFTER MASSIVE FIRE NEARLY DESTROYS CARIBBEAN RESORT; 1,690 EVACUATED "It lit up like a firecracker... people were screaming and crying and running around," Paul Cole, another witness, told 9News. The Badung Fire and Rescue Service said it took more than two hours to put out the flames and there were no casualties, according to The Bali Sun. First Inspector I Gede Adi Saputra Jaya of the Denpasar Police, citing statements from witnesses at the scene, told reporters Monday that the fire is "strongly suspected" to have started after a balloon "was hit by a candle flame, causing it to explode and catch fire," the website added. HUNDREDS OF POUNDS OF FIREWORKS EXPLODE, DESTROYING HOMES AND INJURING FIREFIGHTERS "Initial extinguishing efforts using fire extinguishers by restaurant staff were unsuccessful because the fire had already grown large and spread quickly to the thatched roof," he reportedly said. One witness told 9News, "There are the balloons, a lot of explosions, explosion and explosion and explosion, it was just, yeah, it was terrible." "It was just bedlam," added Joe Xuereb, another witness. "As soon as the fire started, people didn’t know what to do." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The restaurant now says on its website that it is "temporarily closed."

articles.title: In 1929, a fisherman built a wooden boat beside the home where he was raising 13 children; nearly a century later, $1.5 million is being raised to restore it
articles.summary: US News: A wooden fishing boat built in 1929 is nearing a major restoration on Martha’s Vineyard,  Massachusetts. The vessel, Little Lady, is the sole remainin.
articles.body: A wooden fishing boat built in 1929 is nearing a major restoration on Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts. The vessel, Little Lady, is the sole remaining wooden fishing dragger in New England and has been part of the island’s fishing community for generations.According to the Martha’s Vineyard Times, Little Lady is expected to be moved from Ralph Packer’s dock in Vineyard Haven to the Gannon and Benjamin Marine Railway in about a month, where work on the vessel will begin.The full restoration is estimated to cost $1.5 million. The project is being funded through private donations and Community Preservation Act funds from Tisbury and Chilmark. However, $630,000 is still needed to complete the work.After the restoration, Little Lady is expected to serve as an educational hub for younger generations at the docks. Any fish caught using the boat’s drag net will be donated to local food pantries. Nat Benjamin, co-founder of Gannon and Benjamin, describes Little Lady as an “iconic vessel that’s been in Mememsha for many generations.” “We’re trying to keep her there,” he adds.History of 'the little lady'Little Lady was built in Noank, Connecticut, in 1929 by Captain Earl Foster and Oren Olds. The boat was originally named Mary F.Supporters were able to contact Foster’s family and learn more about how the boat was built. According to the family, Foster constructed the vessel beside his family home while raising 13 children with his wife.The boat eventually became so closely connected to the house that the family moved into the woodshed after it was completed. The house was then demolished, and Little Lady was dragged to the shore.By the 1950s, the vessel had been sold to the family of Dennis 'Denny' Jason Jr Jason’s grandfather turned it into a fishing dragger. The boat remained with the Jason family and became closely associated with Menemsha, the historic fishing village on Martha’s Vineyard.Little Lady is recognisable by its red and green-accented hull, ladders running up the centre mast, and its name and number painted in white along the side. Paintings and photographs of the boat have also appeared in local galleries.Restoration replaces much of vesselThe Martha’s Vineyard Fishermen’s Preservation Trust bought Little Lady last year. However, Jason will continue as the boat’s captain after the restoration is completed.According to Shelley Edmundson, executive director of the preservation trust, the boat represents the wider working waterfront community in Vineyard Haven. That community includes ship repair workers, boat builders, fishermen and women, and a fuel station.“We are usually on the docks covered in fish scales, and then you have Gannon and Benjamin here on the waterfront covered in sawdust, and we’re all working really hard to keep our working waterfronts working in different ways. Little Lady symbolizes a wooden boat craftsmanship that is so lively and strong here,” Edmundson says.The remaining money is being raised as supporters prepare for the next stage of the restoration. Edmundson says the next $150,000 raised will be matched by a private donor, closing part of the funding gap.Christian Cabral, who manages operations and the business side of Gannon and Benjamin, outlined the work planned for the boat. Materials have already started to be procured, and the team plans to move Little Lady to the workshop next month.Around 80 per cent of the hull, engine and other parts are expected to be repaired or replaced. At the same time, the restoration team plans to retain the character of the historic vessel.Cabral says, “Restoration, in its broadest sense, is taking an existing object with what now has historic providence, looking at that object, deciding what we need to preserve, how we need to preserve it, and the methodology to take care of it. This is our guiding principle. This is where we start. To put it bluntly, is the object worth saving?” Cabral asks.For those involved with Little Lady, the answer is yes. Cabral says the boat represents the connection between Martha’s Vineyard’s residents and the water, including generations who made their living through fishing and boatbuilding.“Denny and his family, all the community members that go down to Menemsha and get the ice cream at the Galley and see that boat sitting there. The feeling of Martha’s Vineyarders, who have made their money from the water, building boats and fishing, were downstream directly of that lineage. The feeling includes being on board the boat and taking kids out on the water. Those are all worthwhile things that we have the opportunity to preserve,” Cabral says.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: What is Iran’s Castle Breaker missile, used against US bases?
articles.summary: Kheibar Shekan, Iran’s medium-range missile, is said to play a pivotal role in escalating US-Israel tensions.
articles.body:
Iran’s Kheibar Shekan missile, which means Castle Breaker in Persian, has emerged as one of the most talked-about weapons in the US-Israel war on Iran.

The medium-range ballistic missile has been used by Iran in strikes on US military targets and infrastructure in the Middle East this week, as Tehran aims to demonstrate that its missile arsenal remains well-stocked following six months of intermittent US and Israeli attacks.

The war entered a new phase this week following a lull in fighting for a month, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, close to the country’s strategic port of Bandar Abbas, on Monday. That prompted Iran to strike back at US military assets in Jordan.

Since then, the United States has carried out more attacks on various Iranian targets, with Tehran again responding in kind, targeting several US bases in the region, including in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

So, what is the Castle Breaker, what is it capable of, and what is the latest in the US-Israel war on Iran?

What is the Kheibar Shekan or Castle Breaker missile?

It is a medium-range ballistic missile which has been developed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as part of its wider range of missiles .

It is one of Iran’s newer medium-range missile systems, with a range of roughly 1,450km (901 miles), with a payload range (warhead capacity) of 449kg to 590kg (990 pounds to 1,300 pounds).

In comparison, the US has introduced the Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) during the conflict, described by its producer Lockheed Martin as long-range precision-strike missiles that can hit targets ranging from 60km (37 miles) to more than 499km (310 miles) away.

The US has also used Tomahawk cruise missiles, which are long-range, precision-guided weapons that can fly at low altitudes and hit targets up to 2,500km (1,550 miles) away.

The Kheibar Shekan was unveiled in 2022 and takes its name from Khaybar, the word for a fortified settlement associated with early Islamic history. Shekan means breaker or destroyer.

One of the missile’s key characteristics is its solid-fuel propulsion, which allows it to be launched within minutes during a crisis. Solid-fuel missiles are preloaded with fuel, so they do not need to be fuelled just before launch – a process that can take several hours. This makes them easier and safer to operate, less likely to be detected, and they require less logistical support for the transport of fuel.

The fuel is dense and burns rapidly, producing a brief but powerful thrust. It can also be stored for long periods without degrading or breaking down, unlike liquid fuel, which is more prone to deterioration.

Where has Iran used its Castle Breaker missile?

Iran has repeatedly stated that it has been using Kheibar Shekan missiles against US military positions in the region since the six-month conflict began with US-Israeli strikes on Tehran and other sites around Iran on February 28.

State broadcaster IRIB reported that Iranian forces deployed the missile in retaliatory attacks on US assets in Jordan this week.

On July 20, the IRGC released footage showing Kheibar Shekan alongside Fateh-110, Zolfaghar and Emad ballistic missiles being used in attacks on US military targets.

Four days prior, the IRGC said it had targeted a US jet maintenance facility and a new command-and-control centre in Jordan’s Azraq with Kheibar Shekan missiles.

What other missile systems does Iran have?

Iran has a combination of short-, medium- and long-range missiles at its disposal.

Short-range ballistic missiles, which have a range of roughly 150km to 800km (93-500 miles), are built to reach nearby military targets in rapid regional strikes.

Core systems include the Fateh variants: Zolfaghar, Qiam-1 and older Shahab-1/2 missiles. Their shorter range can be an advantage in a crisis as they can be launched in volleys, compressing warning time and making pre-emption harder.

Medium-range ballistic missiles, with a range of roughly 1,500km to 2,000km (900-1,200 miles), include systems such as Shahab-3, Emad, Ghadr-1, the Khorramshahr variants and Sejjil, alongside newer designs like Kheibar Shekan and Haj Qassem.

These missiles put Israeli targets and US-linked sites in the Gulf states within their range.

Iran also has an arsenal of cruise missiles such as Soumar, Ya-Ali, the Quds variants, Hoveyzeh, Paveh and Ra’ad. The Soumar has a range of 2,500km (1,553 miles).

Former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei had previously limited Iranian missile ranges to 2,200km (1,367 miles) but removed that limit following Israel’s 12-day war on Iran in June 2025.

The latest escalation has brought a period of relative calm to an end.

The US resumed attacks on Iranian targets on August 31, with US Central Command saying it had struck IRGC sites in southern Iran.

Iran responded with missiles and drones against US forces and military assets located in the region. On Tuesday, the US military said it had completed another wave of strikes against Iranian military targets.

Tehran reported that the US had also struck civilian targets, including a house which was bombed during a wedding celebration in the city of Kuhestak, killing at least five people and injuring 68, including women and children.

Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq’s Erbil in response.

US President Donald Trump previously threatened more attacks if Iran retaliated, while Tehran said it would also respond to US attacks.

The renewed fighting has also put the Strait of Hormuz back at the centre of the crisis as Iranian and US forces vie for control of the critical waterway.

Oil prices rose sharply this week as markets reacted to the renewed US-Iran fighting and the risk to energy shipments through the key waterway, through which 25 percent of the world’s oil and petroleum products are shipped in peacetime.

The US attacks come shortly after Washington announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, declaring that it would target its financial interests across the world.

articles.title: Ariana Grande tearfully ends 41-show tour and steps back from public life
articles.summary: A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid farewell to her fans as her 41 show tour concluded in London and she began her planned withdrawal from public life.
articles.body: LONDON — A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid a temporary farewell to her fans as her 41-show “Eternal Sunshine Tour” concluded in London on Tuesday night, kickstarting her planned withdrawal from public life. Addressing the audience in London’s famed O2 arena, the pop singer said she was “grateful” to her fans for making her show “so special.” “This has been one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life,” Grande said, dressed in black and perched on a stool on stage. “I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely.” “I’ll cherish this experience always,” she added. Grande, known for hits including “thank you, next” and “hate that i made you love me,” made global headlines in August when she said she would be taking a “step back from visibility” following “public scrutiny.” The announcement came after the release of her latest music video, “petal,” which reignited a public debate about her health. Representatives for Grande said last month that she was looking forward to finishing her tour “on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.” Grande concluded her tour in knee-high boots rather than her signature heels after stating she was “bandaged up underneath” following a “deep cut” on her foot, which she called a “minor injury.” Grande’s “Eternal Sunshine Tour,” which promoted the 2024 album of the same name, began in Oakland, California, in June. She previously labeled the shows “one last hurrah” and has expressed her desire to take on more acting roles. Grande was nominated for an Oscar for her performance as Glinda in the hit musical movie “Wicked.” She had been set to reunite with “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey in a revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” in London next summer, before she pulled out last month. In a statement Tuesday on Instagram, Bailey said he has also decided to “step back” from the Sondheim show. He added that “Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering.”
